properties.description: Anthony, 2026-07-25: "you have requirements A and C, but you missed B." A genuinely different kind of gap from everything detect_gaps finds today. Every existing gap source reasons about STRUCTURE — this requirement has no capability, this capability has no check — and each is deterministic because the hole is visible in the graph's shape. A missing requirement is invisible in the shape: the design is perfectly coherent without it, which is exactly why nobody notices. TWO AXES, and the user's fighter-jet example shows they are different detections. BREADTH is the bigger one: a stakeholder states that the wings must provide X lift and sustain Y G, and the engine must make Z thrust — two SUBSYSTEM-level requirements, which implies a subsystem decomposition in which landing gear, avionics, fuel, flight controls, life support, structures, hydraulics and thermal have nothing whatsoever. That is not interpolating a missing item between two others; it is noticing that 2 of roughly 12 expected subsystems have been named at all, which requires knowing what kind of thing is being built. DEPTH is the second: the wing requirement is itself thin, since wings need more than lift and G-load. Both are semantic — pattern-matching against a domain archetype — so they belong to the LLM half of dec:three-party-checks, not the deterministic core. Bounded accordingly: the agent proposes, the graph records at `proposed`, the human decides, and nothing enters above proposed, or the tool starts inventing intent and dec:human-decides is broken in the way that matters most. cap:requirement-lineage sharpens it considerably — requirement families (which Leiden already clusters, once requirement-to-requirement edges exist) are precisely where an omission is both most likely and most detectable, because a family with two members in a design whose siblings have twenty is visible without knowing any domain at all. PLANNED.
properties.name: Notice the requirement nobody wrote down
